slides.say: Given: x times y is smaller than zero, and y is smaller than the absolute value of y. Which of the following is necessarily true?

So here we have no numbers at all, just signs. And look at the choices, some of them talk about signs and some about sizes. [short pause] We'll solve this two ways, first by understanding the givens, and then by plugging in numbers.

Let's take the givens one at a time. When is x times y negative? Only when they have opposite signs, one positive and one negative. Remember, plus times minus is minus. And if both were positive, or both negative, the product would be positive.
at: Only when they have opposite signs

slides.say: But which one is the negative one? We don't know yet. So let's look at the second given.

When is a number smaller than its own absolute value? Only when it's negative. If y were positive, they'd just be equal, right? Four is equal to its absolute value. But negative four is smaller than four.
So y is negative, and the signs are opposite. And therefore x is the positive one.
[short pause] Now the choices. Number one says x is negative. But we just found that x is positive, so number one is out.

Now careful here, because a lot of students think the negative one is also the smaller one. But the givens only tell us signs, nothing about sizes. So we can't know which absolute value is bigger, and numbers two and three don't have to be true.

Number four says the absolute value of x is equal to x. When is a number equal to its absolute value? When it's zero or positive. And x is positive, so this is always true. So number four is our answer.

[pause] Now our second method, plugging in numbers. It's a great safety net when you're not sure. I need numbers that obey both givens, so y is negative and x is positive. Why negative three and eight? Because they're easy, and they stay away from zero, one and minus one.
Number one, x is negative? Eight isn't negative, so it's out. Number two, eight is smaller than three? No, out.
Number three, negative three over eight, in absolute value, is three eighths. That's less than one, so it stays. And number four, the absolute value of eight is eight, so it stays too.
Two choices survive. Can I already circle one and move on? I can't. I need a tie-breaker, so this time I'll make y the bigger one in size. y is negative six, and x is two.
Negative six over two is negative three, and its absolute value is three. That's not less than one, so number three is out. And the absolute value of two is still two. Aaand it's number four, again.

So which way is better? Here understanding is faster, because the signs give it all away. And the numbers are a great check. [short pause] Negative product, opposite signs. A number smaller than its absolute value, negative. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
